1. Purpose and Scope
This policy states the compensation structure, monthly billing quota, and quota-performance assessment procedure
that apply to every internal engineering position at The CFD ME, LLC. It supersedes rev 2 in its entirety.
The scope covers every W-2 engineering role — owner and principal engineer, technical director and reviewing
engineer, senior CFD engineer, and CFD engineer — whether resident in the Tucson office or working remotely. It
does not apply to contracted outside labor engaged under separate work orders, nor to non-engineering
administrative staff.
The policy is one of three internal-HR documents that jointly govern engineering-side quota, remediation, and
staffing. It is designed to be read alongside the Quota Remediation Procedure rev 2 and the Staffing and Assignment
Sheet.

2. Billing Quota
Each internal engineer carries a monthly billing quota of $20,000/month. Billable work is defined as engineer-hours
logged against a signed and current client engagement, at the billing rate for that engagement.
The quota is a floor, not a target ceiling. It is set at a level the firm has confirmed to be achievable given normal
workload allocation and the firm's active book of business, and is unchanged from the level in effect since the firm
staffed up beyond a single-owner configuration.

3. Definitions of Billable Work
Billable work is engineer-hours logged against an external client engagement where all of the following conditions are
met:
• The engagement is under a signed statement of work, master services agreement, or task order in force at the
   time the hour is logged.
• The engagement is current — not closed, not suspended for non-payment, and not out of scope of any active task
   order.
• The hour is charged at the billing rate designated for that engagement in the governing contract.
The following categories of work are explicitly not billable and do not count toward the quota:
• Internal training, including internal seminars, reading time on external standards, and mentoring or onboarding of
   other firm engineers.
• Firm standards work, including drafting, revising, and reviewing internal modeling standards, QA procedures, and
   standard operating procedures.
• Administrative work, including timesheet entry, expense reporting, procurement, and internal record-keeping.
• Marketing and business development, including proposal preparation, prospect calls, conference attendance, and
   outreach.
The above categories may be excluded from the non-billable list on a case-by-case basis when a specific internal
charge code has been designated for a defined initiative and communicated in writing by the owner. Absent such
designation, they are non-billable.

4. Compensation Structure
Compensation for internal engineering staff has two components:
• Base salary. Set by role and by written offer letter or subsequent written adjustment. Paid semi-monthly. The
   base salary is not tied to individual billed revenue.
• Firm-wide profit share. Distributed on a firm-wide basis according to the profit-share schedule maintained by the
   owner. All internal engineers who are employed at the close of the applicable distribution period participate. The
   profit-share pool is a function of firm profitability, not of any individual engineer's billed revenue.


--- page 2 ---
There are no individual commissions for internal engineers other than the reviewer commission for Marguerite Falk,
PE, described in her role letter and cross-referenced in Section 7. No individual engineer receives a percentage of the
revenue they personally bill.
The firm has deliberately declined to compensate engineers on personal-billing commission. Commission structures
introduce incentive tension between billable-work volume and engineering-work quality, which the firm has
determined it will not accept on the technical side of the practice.

5. Quota Performance Assessment
Quota performance is assessed monthly at close (last business day of each calendar month) by the operations lead
against the billing records in Firm/HR/Billing/. Two consecutive months below quota trigger the Quota Remediation
Procedure (rev 2 or current).
The operations lead's assessment reads the billed-revenue-by-engineer sheet as of the close of the calendar month,
compares each engineer's billed revenue for that month against the $20,000/month quota, and marks each engineer
as met or below for that month. The assessment is a mechanical read of the billing record. It is not a subjective
judgment about the engineer's work.
When an engineer is marked below for two consecutive months, the assessment routes the matter to the Quota
Remediation Procedure for opening of the remediation ladder. No other assessment output — verbal, written, or
otherwise — is used to initiate a response to a quota shortfall.

6. Remediation Procedure
The Quota Remediation Procedure establishes the sole firm response to consecutive quota shortfalls; consult that
document for the applicable ladder. Rung ordering is strict and rungs may not be skipped.

7. Reviewer Compensation Note
Marguerite Falk, PE serves as the firm's Technical Director and Reviewing Engineer and is compensated in part on
commission as a declared incentive under the terms of her role letter. The declared incentive tension between the
commissioned component of her compensation and her role as mandatory review gate on stamped deliverables is
managed through the stamp boundary: Gordon Selby, PE stamps CFD thermal analysis only; fire-resistance ratings
are certified separately by others (Ironwood Fire Protection Engineering). The stamp boundary is stated on every
CFD thermal deliverable that leaves the firm.
The reviewer-commission arrangement is limited to Marguerite Falk's role and is not extended to other internal
engineers. No other internal engineer receives a commissioned component of compensation.
The billing quota, monthly assessment, and remediation triggers are governed per Section 5 above.

8. Records
The following records are maintained in support of this policy:
• Engineer billing records by month. File: /Firm/HR/Billing/billing_by_engineer_2025.xlsx (current
   calendar year) and prior-year archives in the same directory. Maintained by the operations lead. Records billed
   revenue by engineer by month.
• Monthly quota-close assessments. Recorded by the operations lead on the last business day of each calendar
   month; retained in the HR file for the engineer.
• Remediation ladder records. When a remediation ladder is opened, the record of each rung's action, cycle
   duration, and outcome is maintained per the Quota Remediation Procedure rev 2.
• Role letters and compensation adjustments. Retained in each engineer's HR file.
Records are retained for the duration required by applicable law and by firm policy, whichever is longer. Access is
limited to the owner, the operations lead, the individual engineer for that engineer's own records, and Marguerite Falk
in her capacity as Technical Director for records relevant to a remediation ladder she is administering.

Quota Remediation Procedure | rev 2 | Effective 07/01/2025

Principal Engineer)
Applies to: all internal engineering staff of The CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC (trade name: The CFD ME)


1. Purpose
This procedure defines the strict ladder to be followed when the firm's Compensation and Quota Policy rev 3
triggers remediation for an internal engineer. It supersedes rev 1 in its entirety.
The firm's position on quota-shortfall response is stated in the compensation policy and repeated here so that any
operations lead, reviewing engineer, or owner who administers a ladder can read this document standalone: a
shortfall in billed revenue is first a question about assignment, staffing, and the composition of the firm's book of
business, and only after the full ladder has been worked does it become a question about the engineer's fit at the firm.
The ladder set out in Section 3 is the sole response protocol. It is a strict ordered sequence — the rungs are
numbered, and the numbering is normative, not descriptive.
The purpose of this document is to remove discretion at the point of decision. When the compensation policy's
monthly assessment routes a matter to remediation, the response is set: the operations lead opens the ladder at rung
1, works it through a full assessment cycle, and escalates to the next rung only if that cycle does not resolve the
shortfall. There is no branch, no substitution, and no first-response termination.

2. Trigger
The remediation ladder opens when the monthly quota-close assessment under Compensation Policy rev 3 §5
records two consecutive months below the billing quota for the same internal engineer. The billing quota is
$20,000/month per engineer, defined in Compensation Policy rev 3 §2.
The trigger is mechanical. It is read from the billed-revenue-by-engineer sheet maintained in /Firm/HR/Billing/
on the last business day of each calendar month. When the second consecutive below-quota month closes, the
operations lead routes the matter to this procedure and the ladder opens at rung 1. No other input — verbal report,
subjective assessment, client feedback, or peer complaint — opens the ladder.
The trigger is quota-specific. This procedure addresses billed-revenue shortfalls only. Concerns about engineering
quality, professional conduct, or fitness for duty are handled through separate channels and are not within the scope
of the ladder set out below.

3. Ladder
The ladder has three rungs. Rungs are numbered in strict order and may not be skipped. Each rung must run for
its full assessment cycle before the next rung is considered.

Rung 1 — Reassignment to Physical-Test Contract Management
The engineer is reassigned to manage physical-test contracts (e.g., ASTM E119 test coordination, wind-tunnel
campaign management, third-party lab liaison). During this rung the engineer is measured on the validation
schedule (on-time completion of test milestones, cleanliness of instrumentation and data hand-off, and report
turnaround) rather than the $20,000/month billing quota.
Assessment cycle: one full month.
Rung 1 is opened by a staffing decision memo that identifies the engineer, cites the below-quota months of record,
names the specific physical-test contract slot the engineer is being reassigned into (drawn from the Staffing and
Assignment Sheet), and states        the start date of the assessment cycle. The engineer's base compensation is
unchanged during this rung. The billing quota does not apply while the engineer is in rung 1; billing performance
during this cycle is not assessed.
At the close of the one-month assessment cycle, the operations lead records the validation-schedule outcome — met
or below — in the engineer's HR file. If the engineer meets the validation schedule for the cycle, the ladder closes and
the engineer either continues in the physical-test contract slot or returns to standard engagement assignment, at the


--- page 2 ---
owner's discretion. If the validation schedule is not met, the ladder advances to rung 2. Advancement requires a new
staffing decision memo citing rung 2.

Rung 2 — Technical Sales Rotation
If rung 1 does not resolve after a full assessment cycle, the engineer is moved into a technical sales role with an
annual booked-revenue target of 3× base salary. Base compensation remains unchanged during this rung.
Assessment cycle: one calendar year.
Rung 2 is opened by a staffing decision memo that identifies the engineer, cites the rung 1 outcome, names the
technical sales slot (drawn from the Staffing and Assignment Sheet), states       the annual booked-revenue target
expressed as 3× the engineer's current base salary, and states the start date of the twelve-month assessment cycle.
During rung 2 the engineer is measured on booked revenue against the annual target; the $20,000/month billing
quota does not apply, and validation-schedule metrics do not apply.
At the close of the twelve-month cycle, the operations lead records the booked-revenue outcome in the engineer's
HR file. If the annual target is met, the ladder closes and the engineer continues in the technical sales role or returns
to standard engagement assignment, at the owner's discretion. If the annual target is not met, the ladder advances to
rung 3. Advancement requires a new staffing decision memo citing rung 3.

Rung 3 — Offboard
If rung 2 does not resolve after a full year, the engineer is offboarded with standard severance and reference
support.
Rung 3 is opened by a staffing decision memo that identifies the engineer, cites the rung 2 outcome, states the
offboard date, and confirms severance and reference-support terms per the firm's standard offboarding schedule.
The memo is countersigned by the owner.

4. Rules of the Ladder
Rungs shall not be skipped. Each rung must run for a full cycle before the next is considered. Termination is not
available as a first response to a quota shortfall. Generic Performance Improvement Plans are not used.
The rules of the ladder are absolute:
• Order. The rungs run in the order 1 → 2 → 3. Rung 2 may not be opened without a completed rung 1 cycle
   recorded in the HR file. Rung 3 may not be opened without a completed rung 2 cycle recorded in the HR file.
• Full cycle. Rung 1 is one full month. Rung 2 is one full calendar year (twelve consecutive months from the start
   date named in the rung 2 memo). A rung is not "worked" until its full cycle has elapsed. Early advancement is
   prohibited.
• No skipping. No rung may be omitted. There is no discretionary shortcut from rung 1 to rung 3, and no shortcut
   from the trigger directly to rung 2 or rung 3.
• No first-response termination. Offboarding is available only at rung 3, and only after rungs 1 and 2 have each
   run to completion without resolution.
• No generic PIP. The firm does not use generic Performance Improvement Plans for quota shortfalls. The ladder
   set out in Section 3 is the sole response. A PIP is not substituted for a rung, appended to a rung, or issued in
   parallel with the ladder.
• Base compensation. Base salary is unchanged during rungs 1 and 2. The ladder does not adjust base
   compensation; it adjusts assignment and the metric against which the engineer is measured.
These rules are set to remove the two failure modes the firm has determined it will not accept: skipping to termination
without giving the engineer's assignment and staffing a fair chance to correct, and papering over an assignment or
staffing problem with a generic improvement plan that shifts the burden onto the engineer.

5. Records and Documentation
Each rung is opened by a staffing decision memo authored by the operations lead and countersigned by the owner
(Gordon Selby, PE) and, at rungs 1 and 2, by the Technical Director (Marguerite Falk, PE) in her administering
capacity. The memo cites:


--- page 3 ---
• The rung invoked (1, 2, or 3), by number.
• The assessment cycle applicable to that rung (one month for rung 1; one calendar year for rung 2; not applicable
   at rung 3 — the memo states the offboard date instead).
• The confirmed staffing slot for the engineer at rungs 1 and 2, drawn from and cross-referenced to the Staffing and
   Assignment Sheet           (/Firm/Ops/CFDME_staffing_assignments.xlsx). The memo states the
   specific validation-schedule slot for rung 1 or the specific technical sales slot for rung 2.
• The below-quota months of record that triggered the ladder (for the rung 1 memo), or the prior-rung outcome (for
   the rung 2 and rung 3 memos).
• The start date of the assessment cycle.
Staffing decision memos are retained in the engineer's HR file at /Firm/HR/ for the retention period stated in the
compensation policy. At the close of each rung's assessment cycle, the operations lead records the outcome — met
or below — in the same file, alongside the memo that opened the rung. When a ladder closes at any rung, the closure
is recorded in the HR file.
Access to remediation ladder records is limited to the owner, the operations lead, the engineer for that engineer's own
records, and the Technical Director in her capacity administering a ladder.

6. Related

   Defines       the $20,000/month billing quota, the monthly quota-close assessment, and the
   two-consecutive-months-below trigger that opens this procedure. States the firm's position that generic

[9] This memo is issued under CFDME-QA-VAL-002, Validation QA Procedure — ASME V&V 20, rev 2, effective 05/01/2025 (the “Validation Procedure”). Section 3 fixes the reporting form E = S − D with the sign retained; §4 fixes u_val; §5 fixes the acceptance criterion and the secondary comparison to u_val; §6 fixes the source of D; §7 limits E119 conclusions; §9 fixes the stamp block. The Phase 1 SOW §7 invokes ASME V&V 20 and ASTM E119 and states that E119 endurance is not a wildfire survival prediction. The Red Butte report is the certified third-party test of record; the Ironwood memorandum is the certification of record.
[10] No superseded or cancelled document is relied on. RevD is later than revC, but it is not the geometry that was meshed and analysed; using it for future work would require a change order under SOW §8. The Rennert email is a client transmittal, not a laboratory revision.
[11] 3. Assembly identity: run versus certification
[12] Table 1. Certified geometry versus the run geometry and the later revD transmittal.
[13] Conclusion: yes — the run is the certified assembly construction, within the certification’s tabulated scope. Ironwood §1.2 states that any deviation from the tabulated geometry places the assembly outside the certification. Every tabulated parameter matches revC and the Rev A drawing. The Red Butte specimen was 3.05 m × 3.05 m, while revC is a 1830 mm × 2745 mm × 305 mm panel. The certification table does not make plan size a scope parameter; the comparison here is the through-wall construction and tie schedule. If the certification is later read as requiring the 3.05 m plan size, that is a question for Ironwood, not a basis for this validation. The comparison therefore addresses the through-wall construction and tie schedule, not specimen-size or edge effects.
[14] RevD is not the run geometry. It adds a continuous hollow parapet of 610 mm, bringing total height to 3355 mm, with a 50 mm coping cap and 25 mm drip overhang. It was transmitted by Trevor Buckhalter at 16:12 on 10/09/2025, after the revC mesh build on the morning of 10/09/2025. All case logs, the three-grid study and the deliverable manifest cite revC. RevD is therefore not the as-tested or certified geometry, and it is not the geometry of the companion run.
[15] 4. Governing criterion and validation rollup
[16] 4.1 Run result and criterion times
[17] The companion file reports absolute unexposed-face temperatures on an initial ambient of 21.0 °C. The CSV header maps T_unexposed_avg_C to the Red Butte nine-thermocouple average criterion and T_unexposed_max_C to the single-point criterion over the tie course; I used those columns. The single-point criterion is a rise of 181 °C, i.e. 202 °C absolute; the average criterion is a rise of 139 °C, i.e. 160 °C absolute. Linear interpolation of the 1-min output gives a single-point crossing at 130.94 min (reported 131 min) and an average crossing at 176.10 min (reported 176 min). The single-point criterion is reached first and governs, exactly as in the test. S = 131 min.
[18] Table 2. Crossing times, not sample values. Run crossings are linear interpolations of the 1-min output; test times are from Red Butte §5.1–§5.3.
[19] 4.2 Error, acceptance criterion, uncertainty and margin
[20] Table 3. Validation rollup in the order required by Validation Procedure §3: S, D, E, u_val, then the criterion comparisons.
[21] In the required single-line rollup: S = 131 min; D = 118 min; E = +13 min; u_val = ±9 min; acceptance criterion |E| ≤ 11.8 min.
[22] The reported E is +13 min at the whole-minute values; the unrounded E is +12.94 min, which is about 11.0% of D against the 10% limit. The sign is positive: the model over-predicts endurance, which is non-conservative for a fire-resistance claim. Either value exceeds the 11.8-min criterion. The largest prediction that would have cleared the primary criterion is 129.8 min; if predictions are stated only in whole minutes, the largest whole-minute prediction that clears is 129 min, because 130 min gives |E| = 12 min > 11.8 min. That 129.8-min value would still be a resolved model error because |E| = 11.8 min > u_val = 9 min. To satisfy both the primary criterion and the secondary u_val test, S must lie between 109 min and 127 min; the current run at 131 min is 4 min above that upper bound.
[23] 5. What the two comparisons say, and where the rework belongs
[24] 5.1 The two comparisons
[25] Table 4. The run reproduces the test’s 45-min separation between criteria; the governing point is about 6 °C further above the mean in the run.
[26] The separation is reproduced to about 0.2 min. That is a strong diagnostic: the model gets the relative timing of the tie-local single point and the global average right, so the metallic tie path is neither omitted nor grossly misrepresented. The governing point sits 91 °C above the nine-point mean in the run versus 85 °C in the test — a 6 °C larger hot-spot margin, consistent with a slightly stronger modelled tie path, not with a 13-min global delay.
[27] 5.2 Diagnosis
[28] Both criteria are displaced by the same +13 min. A tie-only error or a single-point thermocouple-placement error would move the single-point criterion relative to the average and change the 45-min separation. It does not. The model is therefore transferring heat through the wall too slowly overall — or is being driven by too little effective furnace-side heat — in a common-mode way. The likely causes are the global thermal boundary condition, the temperature-dependent solid properties, contact resistance, or the conjugate-heat-transfer mesh, not the tie geometry or the choice of governing point.
[29] 5.3 Where the rework belongs, and whether it has started
[30] The rework belongs in the E119 companion model, not in D, not in the Red Butte test, and not in the wildfire LES matrix. The audit should cover, in this order:
[31] Boundary condition: the imposed furnace-side gas-temperature/heat-flux history and the convective/radiative surface coefficients used on the exposed face;
[32] Properties: temperature-dependent k, ρ and cp for the printed concrete and galvanized steel, the tie–concrete contact resistance, and whether the run used the drawing’s constant nominal values (k = 1.4 W/m·K, ρ = 2200 kg/m³, cp = 900 J/kg·K for concrete; k = 45 W/m·K for steel);
[33] Mesh and interfaces: the conjugate-heat-transfer mesh and solid–fluid interface treatment, including refinement at the tie–concrete embedment;
[34] Initial and boundary losses: the initial/ambient condition and the unexposed-face convective/radiative loss treatment.
[35] The rework product is a documented E119 case setup, a corrected S, and a new E/S/D/u_val rollup under the same procedure. It is not a change to D and it does not require a new physical test.
[36] Has any of this rework started? No, on the record as of 10/10/2025. The only E119 companion artifact on the file server is the results CSV; there is no E119 case setup, run log, grid/convergence study, property audit or boundary-condition audit. The three-grid study is the wildfire plume case (30.1 MW, D* = 3.76 m, fireFoam LES), not an E119 conjugate run. The solve log is the steady desert-fire scoping attempt. CO-002 is a mesh-refinement pass on the wildfire cases 240°/8 m/s and 270°/8 m/s. None of those is E119 rework. No E119 rework has started.
[37] 6. Experimental value adopted and disposition on Bianca’s figure
[38] I adopt D = 118 min. Red Butte §5.2 and §5.3 identify thermocouple 6, positioned over a horizontal 3.8 mm truss-tie course, as the governing single point at 118 min. The nine-thermocouple average reached its criterion later at 163 min and does not govern. Ironwood §2 adopts the same 118 min and certifies the assembly at 1-hour (60 min); it explains that 118 min is 2 min short of the 120-min 2-hour rung.
[39] Table 5. Certified value versus Bianca Rennert’s client amendment.
[40] Disposition on the amended 129 min: rejected for use as D. Validation Procedure §6 permits substitution of a revised D only with: (1) a reissued report from the laboratory of record bearing the same report number with an amendment sequence (for example “-R1”), signed by the laboratory’s authorized signatory and stating the reason for revision; (2) a calibration certificate covering the instrument or measurement whose revision is at issue, with date and calibration-authority reference; and (3) an explicit statement in the reissued report that the revised value supersedes the original for all downstream use. The 10/09/2025 11:42 email and burn_data_original_vs_revised.csv satisfy none of the three. A vendor discussion and a client post-test correction are not a laboratory revision. The original value stands. I have recorded the transmittal; it does not change D.
[41] There is also an independent technical inconsistency. If the average remains 163 min and the single-point value becomes 129 min, the test separation becomes 163 − 129 = 34 min. The run gives 45 min. The run reproduces the certified 45-min separation, not the proposed 34-min separation. That is further evidence that 129 min is not the record to validate against.
[42] If the 129 min were ever substantiated by the required laboratory reissue and a new Ironwood certification, the effect would be as follows. D = 129 min; the single-point criterion would still govern at 129 min (average 163 min); 129 min exceeds the 120-min 2-hour rung, so Ironwood could certify a 2-hour rating. Only Red Butte Fire & Materials Testing can reissue RBFMT-25-0918, and only Ironwood Fire Protection Engineering — Marla Kettering, PE, AZ PE #45106 — can issue or restate the fire-resistance certification. Ocotillo may request those actions, but The CFD ME cannot perform or substitute for either. Under that hypothetical, E = 131 − 129 = +2 min, the criterion would be 12.9 min, and u_val would remain ±9 min; the comparison would pass both tests. That is not the current record. The current certified rating remains 1-hour (60 min).
[43] 7. What this exercise does and does not establish about the wildfire claim
[44] What it establishes: at most, model fidelity against the ASTM E119 furnace exposure of this assembly — and even that is not established because the comparison fails. What it does not establish: wildfire survival time, ignition or ember resistance, performance under wind-driven radiation, flame tilt or firebrands, or superiority to wood-frame construction. There is no wood-frame comparator test or simulation in the record. E119 is a comparative assembly rating under a smooth, fuel-continuous standard furnace curve; it is not a WUI wildfire exposure, and no algebraic manipulation of an E119 endurance yields a wildfire survival time. Validation Procedure §7, the External Standards Digest §4, Ironwood §5.2 and SOW §7 all prohibit translating this E119 result into a wildfire performance figure.
[45] What would close the gap: certified wildfire-phase physical test data on the same assembly, with the exposure measured (heat flux, gas temperature, wind, duration) and the response measured, plus a matched wood-frame comparator if the comparative marketing claim is to be supported. The CFD would then be validated against that wildfire test under the same procedure: D from the certified wildfire test report, S from the wildfire run, E = S − D, u_val from the RSS of u_num, u_inp and u_exp, the primary criterion |E| ≤ 10% of D, the secondary comparison |E| against u_val, and the sign of E discussed. The future comparison must be reported in that S/D/E/u_val table with citations to the run and the test, not as a yes/no or “validated” statement.
[46] One scheduling/scope conflict should also be recorded. SOW §5 calls the 10/27/2025 Red Butte window a confirmatory ASTM E119 test; Phase 1 Report rev B §4.2 calls it a wildfire-phase physical test, and the staffing record (CFDME_staffing_assignments.xlsx, Open Slots) calls it a confirmatory ASTM E119 test. The SOW governs the contract. No such test is in the record today and no new test is available for this memo, so I do not rely on it. If it is run as E119, it could provide a new D for a future E119 validation, but it would not change the present comparison; if it is run as a wildfire test, it could support a future wildfire validation. Either way, the conflicting descriptions need to be reconciled by the project before the window is used in any deliverable.
[47] 8. What this means for the rest of Phase 1
[48] Section 7 of the Phase 1 report can now be completed with a documented non-validation finding using the drop-in text in §9. Section 8 can be written, but it cannot claim E119 validation or wildfire performance. Appendix B remains to be populated after the six production LES runs. The report remains draft and unreviewed until the other checklist items close.
[49] The six-case wildfire LES production, its verification, and the separate SOW §3.2 structural wind-load case continue on their own bases. The E119 finding does not invalidate the wildfire mesh verification, but it means the shared wall thermal model is not validated: through-wall wildfire predictions carry an unquantified model error. The common-mode +13 min E119 offset is a warning, not a transferable correction.
[50] Schedule: the documented-finding path can preserve the 11/07/2025 validation review and Phase 1 delivery date. A rework-and-revalidate path has not started and would put 11/07/2025 at risk; no new runs or tests are available today. The SOW schedules the LES setup memo for 10/20/2025 and a confirmatory window on 10/27/2025, but the SOW and the Phase 1 draft disagree on whether that window is E119 or wildfire-phase; it is not E119 rework and does not cure the current finding. For the November launch, the only certified rating remains 1-hour (60 min); there is no 2-hour rating and no validated-CFD claim on the present record.
[51] One further Phase 1 point is visible in the same record and should not be lost behind the E119 finding. The only archived OAS case setup on file, Case/system_archive/OAS_case_setup_from_DWA.txt, is the Dry Wash aerospace template: steady rhoSimpleFoam/RANS, no combustion, no radiation, adiabatic walls and a 0.4 kg/m³ freestream. It is not an E119 conjugate-heat-transfer setup, and it does not satisfy SOW §3.1 or Modeling Standard rev 4 §§3 and 5–7 for the wildfire LES. The live Case/system/controlDict on file is empty, and no production wildfire case setup is present. That is a separate open items 2, 3 and 5 matter requiring a full physics rebuild; it is not cured by this memo and it means the wildfire LES should not be treated as production-ready on the archived setup.

No unqualified validation claim may be made, and no launch material may describe this run as “validated against the certified test.” The validation disposition is a documented model-error finding, not an acceptance.

The model is therefore transferring heat through the wall too slowly overall — or is being driven by too little effective furnace-side heat — in a common-mode way. The likely causes are the global thermal boundary condition, the temperature-dependent solid properties, contact resistance, or the conjugate-heat-transfer mesh, not the tie geometry or the choice of governing point.

30 'Normal' The rework belongs in the E119 companion model, not in D, not in the Red Butte test, and not in the wildfire LES matrix. The audit should cover, in this order:
31 'List Bullet' Boundary condition: the imposed furnace-side gas-temperature/heat-flux history and the convective/radiative surface coefficients used on the exposed face;

33 'List Bullet' Mesh and interfaces: the conjugate-heat-transfer mesh and solid–fluid interface treatment, including refinement at the tie–concrete embedment;
34 'List Bullet' Initial and boundary losses: the initial/ambient condition and the unexposed-face convective/radiative loss treatment.
35 'Normal' The rework product is a documented E119 case setup, a corrected S, and a new E/S/D/u_val rollup under the same procedure. It is not a change to D and it does not require a new physical test.

CO-002 is a mesh-refinement pass on the wildfire cases 240°/8 m/s and 270°/8 m/s. None of those is E119 rework. No E119 rework has started.

Ironwood §2 adopts the same 118 min and certifies the assembly at 1-hour (60 min); it explains that 118 min is 2 min short of the 120-min 2-hour rung.

Validation Procedure §6 permits substitution of a revised D only with: (1) a reissued report from the laboratory of record bearing the same report number with an amendment sequence (for example “-R1”), signed by the laboratory’s authorized signatory and stating the reason for revision; (2) a calibration certificate covering the instrument or measurement whose revision is at issue, with date and calibration-authority reference; and (3) an explicit statement in the reissued report that the revised value supersedes the original for all downstream use. The 10/09/2025 11:42 email and burn_data_original_vs_revised.csv satisfy none of the three. A vendor discussion and a client post-test correction are not a laboratory revision. The original value stands. I have recorded the transmittal; it does not change D.

Fire Endurance Evaluation of a Non-Load-Bearing Double-Wythe Printed-Concrete Wall
Assembly
Testing conducted in accordance with the methodology described in ASTM E119, Standard Test Methods for Fire
Tests of Building Construction and Materials.
Report Number: RBFMT-25-0918 Test Date: 09/24/2025 Report Issued: 09/24/2025
Conducted For: Ocotillo Additive Structures 3175 S Palo Verde Rd Tucson, AZ 85713
Red Butte Fire & Materials Testing Salt Lake City, UT


TABLE OF CONTENTS
1. Test Standard and Method 2. Specimen Description 3. Instrumentation 4. Test Conduct 5. Results 6. Conclusion 7.
Instrumentation Calibration Certificates Signatures


1. TEST STANDARD AND METHOD
The evaluation reported here was performed in accordance with ASTM E119, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests
of Building Construction and Materials (current edition). One vertical fire-endurance test was performed on the wall
assembly described in Section 2, using the standard time-temperature curve prescribed by ASTM E119. The
exposed face of the assembly was subjected to the E119 standard curve delivered by the laboratory's natural-gas
vertical wall furnace, with furnace temperatures monitored by nine furnace thermocouples symmetrically distributed
on the exposed face per the standard.
The assembly was tested as a non-load-bearing partition. The applicable fire-endurance criteria for a
non-load-bearing wall under ASTM E119 are the following two thermal-transmission conditions on the unexposed
face:
• Average unexposed-face criterion. The average temperature rise measured by nine thermocouples
   symmetrically disposed on the unexposed face of the specimen shall not exceed 139 degC (250 degF) above the
   initial ambient temperature at any point in the test.
• Single-point criterion. The temperature rise at any single thermocouple on the unexposed face shall not exceed
   181 degC (325 degF) above the initial ambient temperature at any point in the test.
Per ASTM E119, the earlier of the two thermal-transmission criteria governs the reported fire endurance for the
specimen.


2. SPECIMEN DESCRIPTION
One 3.05 m × 3.05 m (10 ft × 10 ft) specimen was constructed by the client at the Red Butte laboratory prior to test.
The specimen is a double-wythe 3D-printed concrete wall assembly consisting of two printed concrete leaves
separated by an open-air cavity and connected by continuous truss-type steel ties.

2.1 Concrete leaves
• Number of leaves: two, oriented parallel and in registration.
• Leaf thickness: each leaf 50 mm as printed and cured (siliceous aggregate mix).
• Aggregate: siliceous.
• Placement: wet-on-wet extruded 3D printing; nominal 20 mm bead pitch; leaves printed vertically on the
   specimen frame and cured to the manufacturer's 28-day protocol prior to shipment for test.

2.2 Cavity


--- page 2 ---
• Cavity width: 205 mm between the interior surfaces of the two leaves.
• Cavity contents: open air. No insulation, no fill, no membrane, no fire-stop material was present in the cavity as
   constructed for this test.

2.3 Overall specimen thickness
• Overall: 305 mm (50 + 205 + 50).
2.4 Wall ties
Continuous truss-type (triangular zigzag) ties fabricated from 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized steel wire connect the
two leaves. Tie schedule:
Parameter                                                   Value
Material                                                    Galvanized steel, truss-type (triangular zigzag),
                                                            continuous
Wire gauge                                                  9-gauge
Wire diameter                                               3.8 mm
Vertical spacing                                            600 mm o.c.
Horizontal extent                                           Continuous, full specimen width
Embedment into each leaf                                    25 mm

Ties were placed by the client at each 600 mm horizontal course during printing of the leaves and were embedded 25
mm into the printed concrete on each side.


3. INSTRUMENTATION
Instrumentation on the unexposed face was applied by Red Butte technicians per ASTM E119. All thermocouples
were Type K, 20 AWG, glass-braid insulated, fixed to the unexposed face of the specimen with pads per the
standard.

3.1 Unexposed-face thermocouple layout
Nine thermocouples, designated TC-1 through TC-9, were installed on the unexposed face in the symmetric pattern
prescribed by ASTM E119: one thermocouple at the geometric center of the specimen, four at the midpoints of
imaginary quadrants, and four additional thermocouples such that no thermocouple lies within 305 mm (12 in) of a
specimen edge and thermocouples are approximately equidistant from one another. The average of the readings
from TC-1 through TC-9 is the value used for the average unexposed-face criterion.
A tenth thermocouple, TC-10, was installed as a single-point plotter and continuous strip-chart reference; TC-10
readings are recorded but are not part of the nine-thermocouple average.

3.2 Position of TC-6 relative to tie course
The specimen was surveyed for tie positions before instrumentation was applied. During layout of the nine
unexposed-face thermocouples, thermocouple 6 fell over one of the horizontal courses of steel wall ties: TC-6 is
located directly opposite a 3.8 mm truss-type tie embedded in the outer (unexposed) leaf. This positioning is retained
as the E119 symmetric layout was applied without adjustment; the location is documented in the plan diagram below.

3.3 Plan diagram callout (unexposed face)


--- page 3 ---
UNEXPOSED FACE - PLAN LAYOUT (viewed from unexposed side)

                                          TC-1                     TC-2                      TC-3




                                          TC-4                     TC-5        TC-10         TC-6
                                                                                                                  tie course
                                                                                                                  600 mm o.c.
                                                                                                                  (9-gauge, 3.8 mm)
                                          TC-7                     TC-8                      TC-9




                                      TC-10 (plotter reference, near geometric center) not part of the nine-thermocouple average.


Legend: circle = thermocouple on plain concrete; square = TC-6, positioned over a horizontal truss-type tie course.


The tie course crossing behind TC-6 constitutes a metallic path from the exposed leaf to the unexposed leaf at that
location. Readings from TC-6 are therefore expected to reflect the local thermal signature of that path and are
reported alongside the eight other unexposed-face thermocouples without adjustment or omission.

3.4 Furnace and ambient instrumentation
• Nine furnace thermocouples (TCF-1 through TCF-9) per E119, symmetrically placed within 6 in of the exposed
   face, monitored delivery of the standard time-temperature curve.
• Two ambient thermocouples (TC-A1, TC-A2) recorded laboratory ambient at the unexposed side, from which the
   initial ambient reference used for the rise criteria was derived.
• Initial ambient (average of TC-A1, TC-A2 at t = 0): 21.0 degC.
3.5 Data acquisition
All thermocouple channels were logged at 1 Hz to a computerized data acquisition system with NIST-traceable
channel calibration. TC-10 was additionally recorded on an independent single-point strip-chart plotter to provide a
mechanical secondary trace.


4. TEST CONDUCT
The instrumented specimen was mounted in the laboratory's vertical wall furnace on the morning of 09/24/2025. The
exposed face was oriented toward the furnace chamber. The specimen was clamped at the perimeter with the same
frame and gasket detail routinely used for non-load-bearing partition specimens at this laboratory.
The furnace was ignited and the exposed face was subjected to the ASTM E119 standard time-temperature curve
from t = 0 onward. Furnace temperatures tracked the standard curve within the tolerance band prescribed by ASTM
E119 for the full duration of the test (deviation area within the specified 10% at 1 hr and 7.5% at 2 hr and beyond).
The specimen was monitored continuously. The test was conducted to termination on the governing
thermal-transmission criterion as defined in Section 1 above; no hose-stream retest was performed as none was
contracted. No load was applied to the specimen (non-load-bearing configuration).
Test start: 09:02 MDT, 09/24/2025. Test termination: 11:00 MDT, 09/24/2025 (118 min after start), at which point the
governing thermal-transmission criterion was reached. Data acquisition continued for 45 additional minutes past
termination to characterize the full unexposed-face response, at which point the average-rise criterion was also
reached (see Section 5).


5. RESULTS
5.1 Average unexposed-face temperature rise (nine-thermocouple mean)
The arithmetic mean of TC-1 through TC-9, expressed as rise above the initial ambient of 21.0 degC, is the value
evaluated against the average criterion.


--- page 4 ---
• Criterion: 139 degC (250 degF) rise above initial ambient.
• The nine-thermocouple mean rise reached 139 degC at 163 min after test start.
5.2 Single-point unexposed-face temperature rise
The maximum rise across the nine unexposed-face thermocouples, at each instant, was tracked continuously against
the single-point criterion.
• Criterion: 181 degC (325 degF) rise above initial ambient.
• The maximum rise reached 181 degC at 118 min after test start.
• Governing thermocouple at the moment the criterion was reached: thermocouple 6, positioned over a horizontal
   steel tie course as described in Section 3.2 and shown in the plan diagram.
At 118 min, TC-6 recorded 181 degC rise above ambient while the nine-thermocouple mean rise stood at
approximately 96 degC. The remaining eight unexposed-face thermocouples (TC-1 through TC-5 and TC-7 through
TC-9) had not individually reached the single-point limit at that time. TC-10 (single-point plotter, near geometric
center) tracked closely with the mean of TC-1 through TC-9 throughout.

5.3 Governing endurance
Per ASTM E119, the earlier of the two thermal-transmission criteria governs the reported fire endurance:

 Criterion                                Value                                    Time reached
 Average unexposed-face rise              139 degC                                 163 min
 (nine-TC mean)
 Single-point rise (any single TC)        181 degC                                 118 min (at thermocouple 6)

The single-point criterion was reached first at 118 min and therefore governs the reported fire endurance for this
specimen.
> Reported endurance D = 118 min.


6. CONCLUSION
Under the conditions of ASTM E119 (standard time-temperature curve, non-load-bearing, no applied load, no
hose-stream retest contracted), the double-wythe 3D-printed concrete wall assembly described in Section 2 exhibited
a measured fire endurance of 118 min, governed by the single-point criterion at thermocouple 6, which was
positioned over a horizontal truss-type steel tie course. The average unexposed-face criterion was reached later at
163 min and does not govern.
This report documents the measured thermal-transmission behavior of the specimen tested. Certification of a
fire-resistance rating for the assembly is the domain of the certifying fire-protection engineer of record for the project
and is not within the scope of this laboratory or this report.

#42798) Supersedes: CFDME-QA-VAL-001 (rev 1, Effective 03/01/2024) Approved: Gordon Selby, PE — Owner &
Principal Engineer (AZ PE #48213)


1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure governs how validation is performed, evaluated, and reported for every deliverable of The CFD
Mechanical Engineer, LLC ("The CFD ME") that carries a validation claim. A validation claim is any statement,
quantitative or qualitative, that a simulation prediction reproduces a physical measurement within a stated tolerance.
Whenever such a claim is made — in a client report, a peer-review response, a testimony exhibit, or an internal
working record — the reasoning, arithmetic, and acceptance decision shall follow the steps set out here.
The scope covers all CFD analyses executed by staff engineers, remote engineers, and contracted vendors of the
firm, regardless of solver stack, regime, or client. It applies from the moment a validation reference is selected for a
project until the corresponding project file is closed and archived. Deviation from this procedure requires a written
waiver signed by both the reviewing engineer of record and the firm's owner, filed to the project's QA folder before the
deliverable is issued.
The procedure does not certify third-party test data, nor does it substitute for the engineering judgment of the
professional engineer of record. It fixes the form in which validation is expressed and the criterion against which it is
judged; it does not relieve any engineer of independent responsibility for the underlying analysis.

2. References
The following external standards inform this procedure. The firm holds single-user licenses to each; proprietary text is
not reproduced. The provisions relied upon are restated below in the firm's own words with citations back to the
source clause.
• ASME V&V 20-2009 (R2016), Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics
   and Heat Transfer. Framework for expressing validation as a comparison error with an associated validation
   uncertainty. See ASME V&V 20 Section 1 (validation framework and definitions) for the source
   formulation restated in Section 3 below, and Section 5 for the components combined in Section 4 below.
• ASTM E119-24, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials. Referenced
   for the exposure curve and the two thermal-transmission end-point criteria applied by testing laboratories. See
   ASTM E119 Section 8 (thermal transmission on the unexposed face · average rise and single-point) for the
   criteria whose interpretation is restated in Section 7.
• NIST NCSTAR 1-5 series, Fire Investigation of the World Trade Center Disaster, thermal-model validation
   appendices. Cited for community practice on uncertainty accounting in conjugate fire-thermal problems; not
   binding.
• Internal: CFD Modeling Standards - Fire & Buoyant Flows (M. Falk, PE); QA Verification Standard -
   Mesh & Resolution (M. Falk, PE); External Standards Digest (M. Falk, PE).

3. Model-Error Formulation
Validation shall be reported as the model error E = S - D with its validation uncertainty u_val, and never as a yes/no.
• S is the simulation prediction — the value produced by the CFD run using the model, mesh, solver, boundary
   conditions, and material properties documented in the report.
• D is the certified experimental value — the corresponding measurement produced by the physical test of record,
   drawn from the certified third-party report described in Section 6.
• E carries a sign. A positive E denotes a simulation that predicts more of the measured quantity than the test
   observed; a negative E, less. The sign is retained through every downstream comparison and is required in every
   rollup.
The equation E = S - D is the reporting form. Every deliverable that carries a validation claim shall present S, D, E,
and u_val in a single line or table, in that order, with a citation to the physical test report from which D is taken and to


--- page 2 ---
the run identifier from which S is taken. Descriptive words such as "matches," "agrees," "confirms," or "is validated"
are inadmissible substitutes for the numerical statement. The reviewing engineer shall reject any submitted
deliverable that omits any of the four quantities or that replaces the numerical rollup with a qualitative
characterization.
The requirement to report E with u_val — rather than a binary outcome — is not a matter of firm style. A yes/no
verdict conceals the sign and magnitude of the discrepancy, hides whether the disagreement is within measurement
scatter or resolved as a model error, and forecloses the diagnostic reasoning the validation exercise exists to support.
The reviewing engineer shall enforce the reporting form on every deliverable.

4. Uncertainty Build-Up
The validation uncertainty u_val is the root-sum-square (RSS) combination of three independent components, each
expressed in the units of the quantity being validated:
1. Numerical uncertainty, u_num. Reflects discretization, iterative convergence, and round-off contributions in S.
For the class of problem addressed in Section 8 — a conjugate thermal simulation of a compartment-wall assembly
under an ASTM E119 exposure — the firm's default value is ±4 min, established from prior three-grid conjugate
thermal studies on similar assemblies. A project-specific value shall be substituted where a resolution study or
convergence study supports one. 2. Input uncertainty, u_inp. Reflects propagation of uncertainties in material
properties (temperature-dependent conductivity, density, specific heat), boundary conditions (furnace-side
temperature histories, ambient side convective and radiative loss), and geometric idealization (leaf thickness, tie
diameter and spacing, cavity dimension). The firm's default value for the same class of problem is ±6 min. 3.
Experimental uncertainty, u_exp. Reflects instrument, calibration, and placement contributions to D as reported by
the testing laboratory. For calibrated Type-K thermocouples of the class used in ASTM E119 furnace work, the firm's
default value is ±5 min.
Combining by root-sum-square:
  u_val = sqrt( u_num^2 + u_inp^2 + u_exp^2 )
  = sqrt( 4^2 + 6^2 + 5^2 )
  = sqrt( 16 + 36 + 25 )
  = sqrt( 77 )
  = ±8.77 min
The result is reported to whole minutes: u_val = ±9 min for this class of problem.
Two guardrails apply.
First, the three components must be independent. If the numerical model uses lab-measured material properties
whose uncertainty is already folded into D, that property uncertainty shall not be double-counted in u_inp. The
reviewing engineer shall verify independence at the peer review stage.
Second, the default values shall be reviewed at least annually or whenever a project uses a materially different
assembly, exposure, or instrument class. A project-specific tabulation of u_num, u_inp, u_exp shall be recorded in
the project QA folder before u_val is published.

5. Acceptance Criterion
The firm acceptance criterion is |E| ≤ 10% of D.
The criterion is scaled: it grows with the endurance value being validated, so short endurances demand tighter
agreement in absolute minutes and long endurances tolerate more. A 30-minute endurance carries a 3-minute band;
a 120-minute endurance carries a 12-minute band; a 240-minute endurance carries a 24-minute band. This scaling is
deliberate. Absolute-minute criteria are unstable across the range of assemblies the firm analyzes; a 5-minute
absolute tolerance is loose against a 30-minute rating and severe against a 4-hour rating. A percentage-of-D criterion
is stable across the range and disciplines short-endurance work where the absolute stakes are largest.
Two secondary tests accompany the primary criterion and shall appear in every validation rollup:
• Compare |E| to u_val. If |E| ≤ u_val, the discrepancy is within the combined validation uncertainty and is best
   characterized as measurement-plus-model scatter. If |E| > u_val, the discrepancy is resolved as a model error —
   larger than the noise floor of the exercise — and shall be treated as an actionable finding, regardless of whether


--- page 3 ---
   the primary 10% criterion is met.
• Compare the sign of E to the direction of the physical expectation. A simulation that consistently over-predicts
   endurance carries different engineering implications from one that consistently under-predicts; the sign is
   preserved in every rollup and discussed in the report narrative.
A deliverable in which |E| exceeds the criterion, or in which |E| exceeds u_val, or both, shall not be released with an
unqualified validation claim. The reviewing engineer determines whether the deliverable may be released with a
documented finding, whether the model shall be reworked, or whether the validation reference itself is unsuitable and
a different reference shall be sought.

6. Source of D
D shall be taken from the certified third-party test report of record. Client-amended values may not be
substituted for D absent a reissued report from the testing laboratory of record and a calibration certificate authorizing
the revision. Post-test amendments transmitted by the client but not authorized by the lab are not admissible as D.
The rule is strict for a reason. D is the physical anchor of the validation; if D moves for any reason other than a
documented laboratory action, the validation ceases to be against the physical test and becomes a comparison
against a preferred number. The two states are indistinguishable in the report if the substitution is silent, and the
record of the exercise is corrupted.
The following forms of documentation are required to substitute a revised D:
1. A reissued report from the testing laboratory of record, bearing the same report number as the original with an
amendment sequence (e.g., "-R1"), signed by the laboratory's authorized signatory, and stating the reason for the
revision. 2. A calibration certificate covering the instrument or measurement whose revision is at issue, with a date
and calibration-authority reference sufficient to trace the correction. 3. An explicit statement, in the reissued report,
that the revised value supersedes the value in the original report for all downstream use.
Absent any of the three, the original value stands. The reviewing engineer shall reject any deliverable that draws D
from a client-amended figure not backed by the above documentation. A polite, specific, thermocouple-calibration
explanation transmitted by a client is not a laboratory revision; the analyst shall record the client transmittal in the
correspondence folder and continue to use the certified D. Any pressure to depart from this rule — from schedule,
from commercial positioning, or from a persuasive account of what "really" happened at the test — shall be resolved
by returning to the reissued-report requirement.

7. Scope Limitation
ASTM E119 exposes an assembly to the standard building time-temperature curve, which is not a WUI
wildfire exposure. E119 endurance is therefore a comparative assembly rating, not a prediction of wildfire survival
time. Validation against E119 data validates the model against E119; it does not validate a wildfire performance
claim.
The distinction is not a formality. The E119 curve is a smooth, monotonically rising fuel-continuous compartment fire
scenario intended to grade the relative thermal performance of building assemblies under a repeatable exposure. A
wildland-urban interface exposure is a wind-driven, radiation-dominated, transient fire-front event whose peak heat
flux, duration, and spatial distribution differ from E119 at every axis. An assembly with a two-hour E119 rating is not
thereby a two-hour wildfire assembly, and no algebraic manipulation of an E119 result yields a wildfire survival time.
Firm practice on this point:
• Reports that use E119 test data to validate a CFD model shall state, in the validation section, that the validation
   exercise establishes model fidelity against the E119 exposure and shall not extrapolate that finding to wildfire,
   hydrocarbon-pool, or other non-E119 exposures.
• Where a project's ultimate objective is a wildfire performance claim, the validation section shall separately identify
   (i) what E119 data validates, (ii) what it does not, and (iii) what additional physical evidence would be required to
   close the gap.
• Marketing or commercial statements that translate an E119 rating into a wildfire performance figure are outside
   the firm's stamp and shall not appear in any firm-issued deliverable.

8. Worked Example — Illustrative Assembly


--- page 4 ---
The worked example below illustrates the arithmetic of Sections 3 through 5 using a hypothetical compartment-wall
assembly. The values used are illustrative and are not the values of record for any live project; they are pedagogic
only.
Inputs (illustrative).
• D = 120 min. Certified single-point endurance drawn from a hypothetical laboratory ASTM E119 report for the
   illustrative assembly. The single-point criterion governs per ASTM E119.
• S = 126 min. Simulation prediction from a conjugate CFD run mirroring the E119 furnace exposure for the same
   illustrative assembly.
• u_val = ±9 min. Per Section 4, using default values (u_num = ±4, u_inp = ±6, u_exp = ±5), combined by
   root-sum-square.
Rollup (illustrative).
• E = S − D = 126 − 120 = +6 min. Reported as E = +6 min, sign retained.
• Primary criterion: 0.10 × D = 0.10 × 120 = 12 min. Comparison: |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min. The primary criterion is
   met.
• Secondary comparison to u_val: |E| = 6 min ≤ 9 min. The discrepancy is within the combined validation
   uncertainty.
Conclusion (illustrative). |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min criterion AND ≤ 9 min u_val. The illustrative simulation would validate
against the illustrative certified test under the primary criterion, with the discrepancy sitting within the combined
validation uncertainty.
The point of the worked example is the arithmetic and the reporting form, not the outcome. In practice the analyst
reads D from the certified third-party report per Section 6, computes S from the run of record, tabulates u_val per
Section 4, and applies Section 5 to arrive at an acceptance decision. The engineering action that follows from a
non-validating rollup — grid resolution review, boundary-condition audit, material-property review, geometric
idealization audit — is not a substitution of D. Section 6 governs D.

9. Stamp Boundary
The CFD analyst of record stamps CFD thermal analysis only. The firm's stamp block on any deliverable that carries
a validation claim under this procedure shall read:
"CFD thermal analysis only. Fire-resistance rating certified separately by others."
Fire-resistance rating certification is reserved to the fire-protection professional engineer of record for the project.
Where the firm's CFD work supports a rating certification issued by a fire-protection PE, the firm's deliverable and the
fire-protection PE's certification remain separately stamped and separately scoped. A CFD validation finding under
this procedure is not a rating action; a rating action is not a CFD validation finding. Neither substitutes for the other,
and neither shall be represented as the other in any client-facing communication.

Ocotillo Additive Structures — WUI Wildfire Exposure, Phase 1
Phase 1 Draft Report — Revision B (Unreviewed)

Project: CFDME-2025-041 — Ocotillo WUI Wildfire, Phase 1
Client: Ocotillo Additive Structures
Report revision: rev B (draft, unreviewed)
Prepared by: Gordon Selby, PE — AZ PE #48213
Date: 10/09/2025

1. Purpose & Scope
1.1 Purpose
This report documents the Phase 1 thermal-CFD analysis of the Ocotillo Additive Structures double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall assembly under Sonoran Desert wildland-urban-interface exposure. The analysis is a large-eddy simulation of a fire-front segment representative of a Sonoran buffelgrass surface fire advancing on the exposed face of the assembly. The exposure envelope, fire-source characterisation, mesh study, and preliminary thermal response are reported here. Companion structural wind-pressure work under SOW Section 3.2 is documented separately.
1.2 Scope
The scope of the Phase 1 analysis is limited to:
Regime classification and selection of solver stack;
Site-envelope characterisation from Pima County ALERT ten-year hourly meteorology;
Fire-source characterisation from published Rothermel / Byram / solid-flame correlations for the specified fuel model;
Large-eddy simulation of the fire-front sub-domain at design-envelope wind speeds and directions;
Thermal treatment of the double-wythe cavity wall assembly per the project case-setup record;
Verification of the LES discretisation on the wildfire sub-domain;
Preliminary reporting of unexposed-face and tie-embedded thermal response.
1.3 Scope exclusions
Fire-resistance rating certification of the assembly is explicitly outside the scope of this report and outside the stamp boundary of The CFD ME. The certified rating for the subject wall assembly is issued separately by others (see the standard stamp block in §9). This report is a computational thermal analysis; it does not certify, extend, or modify any assembly rating.
Structural wind-pressure work per SOW §3.2 is a separate deliverable and is not included here.
2. Governing SOW Reference
2.1 Statement of Work
The governing contract for the analysis reported here is the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1 Statement of Work, CFDME-2025-041, signed 10/08/2025. Two technical sections of the SOW frame the Phase 1 workscope:
2.2 SOW §3.1 — Wildfire Analysis Matrix
Six wildfire-exposure cases, formed as the cross-product of two wind directions and three wind speeds:
Case | Wind direction (deg from N) | Wind speed at 20 ft (m/s)
1 | 240 | 5
2 | 240 | 8
3 | 240 | 12
4 | 270 | 5
5 | 270 | 8
6 | 270 | 12


The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).
2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case
SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22, sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2 structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.
3. Method
3.1 Regime classification
Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4 (§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived here.
3.2 Solver stack
Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet, combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.
3.3 Fire source
The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a 3.0 m segment of the advancing fire front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that segment is 30.1 MW, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this source term are given in §5.
3.4 Wall assembly
The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC: two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling Standard §6.
3.5 Geometry of record
The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and results file in this report references OAS-WUI-01_revC as source geometry. The architectural drawing for the same assembly (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout this report.
4. Assumptions & Limitations
4.1 Assumptions
Fuel model. Sonoran buffelgrass is treated as a continuous, homogeneous surface fuel bed at the fuel load and heat content given in §5. Fuel spatial heterogeneity below the sub-domain footprint is not represented.
Fire-source stationarity. The 3.0 m front segment is held stationary within the LES sub-domain; the wall assembly is at the point of nearest approach for the sampled interval. Fire-front advance across the assembly footprint is not simulated within the sub-domain.
Meteorological stationarity. Inlet wind speed and direction are stationary within each case at the values in the SOW §3.1 matrix; diurnal, gust, and synoptic-scale variability are represented only by the envelope in §5.
Cavity contents. The cavity is modelled as open air with no insulation, per the as-built assembly.
Concrete properties. Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete properties are those in the modeling standard reference table, with temperature dependence enabled; spatial variability introduced by the printing process is not represented.
Radiation participation. Concrete surfaces are treated as grey diffuse emitters at emissivity 0.9, per the radiation model selected in the project case-setup record.
4.2 Limitations
The analysis is a thermal analysis only. It does not certify fire-resistance rating, does not predict structural collapse, and does not predict spalling.
The analysis reports response to the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix. It does not predict survival of the assembly under exposures outside that envelope.
The ASTM E119 furnace exposure is a comparative-rating exposure; a companion E119 simulation is reported under Validation (§7) for model-verification purposes only. E119 endurance is not a wildfire survival prediction.
Validation of the wildfire configuration against a wildfire-phase physical test is scheduled for the Red Butte confirmatory window on 10/27/2025 and is not reported here.
5. Results
5.1 Site design envelope
Ten-year hourly meteorology from the Pima County ALERT network at the Avra Valley WUI site establishes the design exposure envelope:
Quantity | Design range
Wind speed at 20 ft | 5–12 m/s
Ambient temperature | 35–42 °C
Relative humidity | 10–25 %


These ranges bracket the fire-season daytime conditions used for the SOW §3.1 matrix inlets.
5.2 Fire-source characterisation
For the Sonoran buffelgrass fuel model at the site design envelope:
Quantity | Value
Fuel load | 0.6 kg/m²
Heat content | 18,600 kJ/kg
Rate of spread (Rothermel) | 0.9 m/s
Byram fireline intensity | 10,040 kW/m
Solid-flame flame length | 5.4 m (wind-tilted)
LES sub-domain front segment | 3.0 m
LES sub-domain total HRR | 30.1 MW


The 5.4 m solid-flame length is the wind-tilted Byram length. It is shorter than the still-air Heskestad correlation at 30.1 MW / 3.0 m (which would predict ~11.5 m); this gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy.
5.3 Plume dynamics
The plume in every solved case exhibits a well-organised puffing signature at the plume base, with a puffing frequency of 0.87 Hz. The puffing signature is resolved in time by the transient LES; centreline temperature and velocity monitors oscillate at that frequency about their mean values, sampled over no fewer than twenty puffing cycles at t ≥ 8 s.
5.4 Thermal response — preliminary
Preliminary plume-centreline peaks on the fine grid are T_peak ≈ 1461 K and U_z,peak ≈ 12.4 m/s at the reference probe location (0.75·D* above the source top surface). Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories for the six SOW §3.1 cases will be reported in Appendix B upon completion of the production LES runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).
6. Verification
6.1 Three-grid study
A three-grid study was executed on the wildfire sub-domain over the OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry, following the firm's verification reporting layout. Background cell sizes and headline monitors on the plume centreline at t = 40.0 s are:
Grid | Background dx (m) | Cells | T_peak (K) | U_z,peak (m/s) | Puffing period (s)
Coarse | 1.0 | 1,410,240 | 1420 | 12.8 | 1.14
Medium | 0.7 | 4,023,680 | 1487 | 11.2 | 1.15
Fine | 0.5 | 11,196,000 | 1461 | 12.4 | 1.15


Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect ratio) with "Mesh OK." returned by checkMesh on every grid. Transient time stepping per firm standard §4 applies to all three runs; puffing period is recovered on all three grids.
6.2 Grid-to-grid comparison
Grid-to-grid behaviour of the T_peak and U_z,peak monitors is non-monotonic across the three grids. The corresponding puffing-period monitor is essentially converged from the medium grid onward. The fire-source refinement zone carries two additional refinement levels above background on every grid; the ratio of refined-zone cell size to background cell size is preserved across the three cases.
6.3 Selection of reporting grid
The fine grid (background dx = 0.5 m) is retained as the reporting grid for the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases. Detail of the underlying LES resolution figures on that grid is given in Appendix C.
